newsitem.headline: AMLC BEEF WEEKLY - AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES.

AMLC COMMENTARY: The July bull run in beef prices in the U.S. may have run its course. Strong demand over the 4th of July holiday weekend cleaned out inventories and this, coupled with the attractive price of beef compared to alternative meats, encouraged retailers to build promotions around beef. This created strong end-user demand and, as a result, some retailers were caught short of inventory.
The ensuing scramble for supplies pushed boxed beef prices to a year high last week, of 108USc/lb. This aided a 4-5USc/lb rise in U.S. cattle prices to 66-67USc/lb.
Boxed beef prices fell 4-5USc/lb this week, however, as retailer enthusiasm for beef at these higher prices diminished.

The manufacturing beef market was affected by slow foodservice sales and by the possibility that some of the large foodservice chains are thinking about promoting alternatives to beef in upcoming Labour Day promotions.

Historically, grinding beef prices receive a kick in lieu of the Labour day holiday (September 1). This is attributed to increased demand for ground beef for outdoor grilling purposes. Retail buying should begin to pick up in the coming weeks in preparation for this holiday.

Australian beef prices in the U.S. market followed the U.S. domestic grinding beef market down this week. U.S. domestically produced lean manufacturing beef fell 5-11USc/lb. In the spot market, prices for Asutralian product fell by 3-4USc/lb. Prices on forward offers for product now exceed those in the spot market.

In Australia's other major export market, Japan, the news was slightly better this week. Solid gains for grassfed product on Japanese wholesale markets and a further depreciation in the A$ against the yen has led to improvement in export market conditions.

The trade is hoping for solid sales overthe Obon holiday period which will help clean up inventories and lead to firm demand for beef, as stocks are replenished. Forward offers for beef currently exceed spot market prices.

A solid break in the season would limit supplies from Australia substantially. Large kills are currently only being maintained by the forced slaughter of cows and heifers. Many of these cows are reported to be in the advanced stages of pregancy, leading to thoughts about where next year's cattle will be coming from.

Speaking of breaks in the season, it tried to do just that during the week. Falls of up to 25mm were recorded across much of southern Australia, beginning with rain on the coast and in the south-west of Western Australia.
By mid-week, the falls had spread to the lower reaches of South Australia before bringing rain to southern New South Wales and Victoria by week's end.
Most falls were in a range between 10-20mm.
This rainfall will grant some crops and livestock a fortnight's reprieve, however, that is all it will be, unless some more follow-up rain is received soon.

Cattle markets in the north of Australia improved this week. Queensland processors bid export steers and bullocks in Queensland and northern New South Wales to levels not seen since early 1996 (bullocks 110-114c/kglw, medium weight steers 104.5c/kglw).

Towards the south, however as quality deteriorated, markets became harder to read. Prices for good quality stock held their own, although markets were generally dominated by plainer cattle which were discounted. Feedlotters were again active in saleyards and were responsible for propping up the market for cattle in store and forward store condition.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
